questions.q: What does the first 24 bits of a 48-bit MAC address identify?
options: The device's IP address
The manufacturer, via the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI)
The port number it will use
The encryption key for the device
questions.explain: The first 24 bits are the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), which identifies the manufacturer; the last 24 bits are assigned by that manufacturer to make the full address unique.

questions.q: How does a switch decide which port to forward a frame out of?
options: It always floods every frame out every port
It checks its MAC address table; if the destination MAC is known, it forwards only to that port
It asks a router for instructions on every frame
It picks a random port
questions.explain: A switch maintains a MAC address table mapping MAC addresses to ports, learned from source addresses on incoming frames, and forwards known destinations only to the matching port.

questions.q: What does a switch do when it receives a frame for a destination MAC address it hasn't learned yet?
options: It drops the frame silently
It floods the frame out every port except the one it arrived on
It sends the frame back to the source
It converts the frame into a broadcast permanently
questions.explain: An unknown destination causes the switch to flood the frame out every port except the source port — a one-time behavior until it learns the destination's actual port.

questions.q: What is the key functional difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A hub operates at Layer 3, a switch at Layer 2
A hub repeats every frame out every port with no intelligence; a switch learns MAC addresses and forwards selectively
There is no functional difference — the terms are interchangeable
A switch can only connect two devices at a time
questions.explain: A hub has no addressing intelligence and repeats every frame out every port; a switch learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards frames only where they need to go.

questions.q: What actually separates one broadcast domain from another?
options: Switches — every switch creates a new broadcast domain
Routers — they don't forward broadcasts between networks, which is what bounds a broadcast domain
The length of the Ethernet cable
The manufacturer of the network card
questions.explain: All devices connected via switches share one broadcast domain; routers, which don't forward broadcast frames between networks, are what actually separate one broadcast domain from another.
